data.title: Rapamycin increases lifespan and inhibits spontaneous tumorigenesis in inbred female mice
data.authors: Anisimov VN; Zabezhinski MA; Popovich IG; Piskunova TS; Semenchenko AV; Tyndyk ML; Yurova MN; Rosenfeld SV; Blagosklonny MV

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Female 129/Sv inbred mice given rapamycin intermittently (2 weeks per month) from 2 months of age for life; survival, body weight, ageing-rate measures and spontaneous tumours
data.finding: Female 129/Sv inbred mice received rapamycin intermittently, 2 weeks in every month, from 2 months of age for the rest of their lives. Treated mice gained less weight with age, showed a slower estimated rate of ageing, lived longer, with the gain most visible among the last survivors, and developed spontaneous tumours later. 22.9% of rapamycin-treated mice were still alive when the last control mouse died. The paper provided evidence that an intermittent rapamycin schedule can extend lifespan in a normal inbred mouse strain, adding to earlier results in genetically heterogeneous mice. Boundary: Female mice of a single inbred strain (129/Sv) only; drafted from the abstract only, so dose, group sizes and median-lifespan statistics are not given here.
data.abstract_excerpt: The nutrient-sensing TOR (target of rapamycin) pathway is involved in cellular and organismal aging. Rapamycin, an inhibitor of TOR, extends lifespan in yeast, fruit flies and genetically heterogeneous mice. Here, we demonstrate that lifelong administration of rapamycin extends lifespan in female 129/Sv mice characterized by normal mean lifespan of 2 y. Importantly, rapamycin was administrated intermittently (2 weeks per month) starting from the age of 2 mo.

extracted_findings.intervention: Rapamycin, intermittent (2 weeks per month), lifelong from 2 months of age
extracted_findings.effect: Increased lifespan, reduced age-related weight gain, delayed spontaneous cancer
